newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's new peace envoy heads for Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Russia's new peace envoy heads for Chechnya.

text.p: Russia's new security chief, Ivan Rybkin, headed for Chechnya on Sunday to begin his first visit to the breakaway region and talk to rebel leaders worried about the sacking of his predecessor, Alexander Lebed.

"We will talk about the mechanism of a return to peaceful life and what is needed to make economic revival work and ensure people's normal activities," Rybkin told reporters on arrival in Ingushetia, the region neighbouring war-torn Chechnya.
"We will discuss everything in detail and with no haste," he added, but declined to say who he would meet.
In late August Lebed brokered a peace deal between Moscow and the separatists but the rebels say they are worried that his sacking could undermine the peace process.
Rybkin and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin have been at pains to reassure them that Moscow does not want a return to the violence which killed tens of thousands of people.

Instead of travelling straight on to Chechnya, Rybkin spent the day in Ingushetia, visiting a school, printing house and hotel built on the proceeds of a special economic zone set up there, Itar-Tass news agency said.
Meanwhile rebel leaders told a congress in southwestern Chechnya there could be no compromise on independence from Moscow -- the issue which sparked their 21-month conflict with Russian troops.

Conservative Kremlin officals and members of parliament cite such provocative comments to explain their opposition to the August 31 peace deal, which the rebels have treated as a victory in their battle to split Chechnya from Moscow.
The agreement called for the withdrawal of Russian troops and said discussions on Chechnya's future status should be put on hold for five years.

But the rebels later confirmed their plans to seek independence, took Chechnya under their control and unilaterally formed a "coalition government", defying an earlier agreement to cooperate with Russia in creating a post-war authority.

"Chechen independence cannot be subject to trade-offs and compromises," rebel spokesman Ruslan Martagov quoted separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev as telling Sunday's Congress of the Chechen People, Interfax news agency reported.
"After the defeat of the million-strong Russian army, the Chechen people have a right to dictate their conditions to Moscow," Martagov quoted another leader as saying.
Some 1,500 delegates approved plans to hold local elections in January and put forward Yandarbiyev as a candidate for president, Tass said.
Yandarbiyev became rebel leader in April after his predecessor Dzhokhar Dudayev, who declared Chechnya independent in 1991, was reported killed in a Russian rocket attack.

The congress opened in a Grozny building but delegates then moved to Urus-Martan, 35 km (20 miles) southwest of the Chechen capital, following a telephoned bomb warning, Tass said. An initial police search did not find any trace of a device.
Separatist leaders said on Saturday they opposed Moscow's plans to keep two brigades permanently in Chechnya.

The rebels, who saw the peace deal as a face-saving way for Moscow to let Chechnya go, insist all Russian troops should leave. Moscow has ruled out granting independence to Chechnya and the separatists fear hardliners could restart the war.
